entities.name: Henry Polak
entities.intro: Young sub-editor of The Critic in Johannesburg who sought Gandhi out after reading his letter about the plague.

entities.name: Albert West
entities.intro: An Englishman from a Lincolnshire peasant family, partner in a small Johannesburg printing firm. Gandhi's evening walking companion from the vegetarian restaurant.

entities.name: Klipspruit camp
entities.intro: Tent camp outside Johannesburg where the location's residents were moved during the plague.

entities.name: 'Unto This Last'
entities.intro: Ruskin's book on economics and the dignity of labour, given to Gandhi by Polak.

entities.name: Phoenix Settlement
entities.intro: A farm settlement 14 miles from Durban, founded by Gandhi in 1904.

entities.name: Chhaganlal Gandhi
entities.intro: Gandhi's cousin, who works at the Indian Opinion press and has wanted since childhood to work under him.

entities.name: Govindaswami
entities.intro: Machinist at the Indian Opinion press.

entities.name: Millie Polak
entities.intro: Henry Polak's fiancée in England; a Christian by birth.

entities.name: Mrs. West
entities.intro: Albert West's wife, from a Leicester shoemaking family.

entities.name: Mr. MacIntyre
entities.intro: A Scottish theosophist whom Gandhi coached for a legal exam.

entities.name: The Zulu 'Rebellion'
entities.intro: The 1906 Bambatha uprising in Natal, sparked by a new poll tax on Zulus.

entities.name: Satyagraha
entities.intro: 'Truth-force': the method of resisting injustice through truth and nonviolence, willingly accepting suffering.

entities.name: The Durban doctor
entities.intro: A medical friend in Durban who operated on Kasturbai.

chapters.situation: Gandhi and his young helpers have nursed 23 plague-stricken miners through a night in a makeshift ward in the Johannesburg location.
chapters.summary: The municipality provides a dirty warehouse, which the volunteers clean themselves, and a nurse who brings brandy. Gandhi and his helpers refuse brandy. With Dr. Godfrey's permission he treats three patients with wet earth packs; two of them are the only survivors, while the other twenty die. The nurse catches the plague and dies. Gandhi's letter to the press blaming the municipality brings him Henry Polak and Rev. Doke. His dinner companion Albert West offers to nurse; Gandhi instead sends him to run the Indian Opinion press in Durban.

updates.gandhi: Treats plague patients with earth packs; two of the three survive. His press letter wins him new friends.
updates.williamgodfrey: Stays in charge of the plague ward and allows Gandhi's earth treatment for three patients.
updates.west: Offers to nurse plague patients and is sent instead to run the Indian Opinion press in Durban for £10 a month. He becomes 'a partner of my joys and sorrows'.
updates.polak: First mention: drawn to Gandhi by his press letter about the plague.
updates.doke: First mention: partly drawn to Gandhi by his plague letter.
updates.madanjit: Kept busy in Johannesburg, so West takes over the Durban press.
updates.plague: Twenty of 23 patients die. The two survivors had earth treatment. The brave nurse dies.
updates.naturecure: Earth packs on head and chest. Gandhi admits his faith in them has no solid scientific basis.
updates.indianopinion: Albert West takes charge of the press in Durban.

status.west: Running the Indian Opinion press in Durban

chapters.situation: The plague ward is closed, but the municipality now moves to stamp out the plague in the Indian location.
chapters.summary: Gandhi cooperates with the municipality and persuades Indians to accept its measures, averting force. The location is sealed, its residents moved to a tent camp at Klipspruit for three weeks, and the location burned. Many residents kept their savings buried, so Gandhi becomes their banker without fees, depositing nearly £60,000 after disinfecting the coins. The people soon enjoy life in the camp.

updates.gandhi: Persuades Indians to cooperate with plague measures and deposits about £60,000 of their buried savings. Cycles out to the camp daily.
updates.location: Evacuated and burned to the ground after the plague.
updates.klipspruit: Residents live under canvas for three weeks, provisioned by the municipality, and are soon singing and merry.
updates.plague: Contained by evacuation and burning, at great municipal expense.
updates.publicwork: Gandhi's cooperation spares the community the use of force.

chapters.situation: The plague is over and Gandhi's standing with poor Indians is higher than ever, but Indian Opinion's finances are a mess.
chapters.summary: Gandhi befriends Henry Polak at the vegetarian restaurant and finds they share views on the essentials of life. West writes that Indian Opinion is losing money, and Gandhi admits his credulity in trusting Madanjit's estimate. Polak gives him Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' for the 24-hour train to Durban. Gandhi reads it overnight, cannot sleep, and resolves to change his life. He takes three lessons from it: the individual's good lies in the good of all, a barber's work is worth as much as a lawyer's, and a life of labour is the life worth living.

updates.gandhi: Transformed overnight by 'Unto This Last' and resolves to live a life of labour.
updates.polak: Befriends Gandhi and lends him 'Unto This Last', which changes his life.
updates.west: Reports Indian Opinion is losing money but stays on regardless, without complaint.
updates.madanjit: His optimistic estimate of the paper's profits proves wrong.
updates.ruskin: 'Unto This Last' brings an 'instantaneous and practical transformation' in Gandhi's life. He later translates it into Gujarati as 'Sarvodaya'.
updates.unto: The good of each lies in the good of all, all work has equal value, and the life of labour is the life worth living.
updates.truth: Gandhi admits a votary of truth must not state things he has not verified, and that he has never fully overcome his credulity.
updates.indianopinion: Losing money; its books are in disorder.

chapters.situation: Inspired by 'Unto This Last', Gandhi has resolved to live by manual labour, and Indian Opinion is losing money in Durban.
chapters.summary: Gandhi proposes moving Indian Opinion to a farm where everyone does manual work and draws £3 a month regardless of colour. West, Chhaganlal Gandhi and Govindaswami join; Madanjit thinks it folly. Within a week they buy 100 acres at Phoenix, 14 miles from Durban, for £1,000. Rustomji gives building material and Boer War veterans build a press shed in under a month, while everyone lives in tents among the snakes. Maganlal Gandhi leaves his business to join and becomes Gandhi's foremost coworker.

updates.gandhi: Founds Phoenix Settlement in 1904, with equal pay of £3 a month for all.
updates.west: Agrees to the Phoenix scheme and lives in a tent among the snakes while the press is built.
updates.chhaganlal: Joins Phoenix without argument and 'has been with me ever since'.
updates.madanjit: Thinks the Phoenix plan foolish and fears it will ruin the paper.
updates.rustomji: Supplies corrugated iron and building materials for Phoenix.
updates.maganlal: Leaves his business for Phoenix and becomes, by 'ability, sacrifice and devotion', foremost among Gandhi's original coworkers.
updates.phoenix: About 100 acres with a spring and fruit trees, bought for £1,000. A 75-by-50-foot press shed is built in under a month.
updates.unto: Phoenix is Gandhi's attempt to put Ruskin's ideas into practice.
updates.indianopinion: Moves to Phoenix; only one issue is printed elsewhere.

chapters.situation: Phoenix Settlement has just been built and Indian Opinion's press has moved there.
chapters.summary: On the night of the first Phoenix issue, the oil engine refuses to start and West comes to Gandhi in tears. Gandhi wakes the carpenters sleeping on the press floor, who gladly take turns at the hand-wheel with everyone else until 7 a.m., West singing hymns. In the morning the engine starts at the engineer's first touch. The paper goes out on time, and the settlement later gives up the engine altogether.

updates.gandhi: Turns the hand-wheel all night with the carpenters to get out the first Phoenix issue.
updates.west: Despairs when the engine fails, then sings hymns as everyone works the hand-wheel.
updates.phoenix: A night of shared labour sets the settlement's spirit of self-reliance. It later works by hand power alone.
updates.indianopinion: Reduced to foolscap size so it could be printed by treadle in an emergency. The first Phoenix issue goes out on time.

chapters.situation: Phoenix Settlement has published its first issue. Gandhi hopes to retire there and live by manual labour.
chapters.summary: The land is divided into three-acre plots with corrugated-iron houses. Everyone learns typesetting, and Maganlal becomes an expert while Gandhi remains 'a dunce'. Gandhi has to return to Johannesburg. Polak, delighted his book bore fruit, joins Phoenix, but soon agrees to come to Johannesburg as Gandhi's articled clerk since Ritch is leaving for England. MacIntyre joins too. Gandhi realizes he is being drawn deeper into his practice in the name of the simple life.

updates.gandhi: Can stay at Phoenix only briefly before returning to his Johannesburg practice, taking on more clerks.
updates.polak: Joins Phoenix 'like a duck takes to water', then agrees to qualify as an attorney under Gandhi in Johannesburg.
updates.maganlal: Becomes an expert compositor and masters all branches of press work.
updates.naazar: Still editor of Indian Opinion, but stays in Durban and does not join the scheme.
updates.ritch: Leaves to finish his legal studies in England.
updates.macintyre: Joins Gandhi's office as an articled clerk.
updates.phoenix: Three-acre plots, corrugated-iron houses, and everyone learning to set type.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is back in Johannesburg with Polak and MacIntyre as clerks, and has given up hope of returning to India soon.
chapters.summary: Gandhi sends for Kasturbai and the children. On the voyage eight-year-old Ramdas breaks his arm, and Gandhi heals it with daily earth poultices. Polak moves in 'like blood brothers'. Gandhi urges him not to postpone marrying his fiancée for money, and she comes from England. The registrar hesitates because the best man is Indian, until the Chief Magistrate intervenes. West returns from England with a wife and mother-in-law, and Phoenix grows into a little village.

updates.gandhi: Brings his family to Johannesburg. Treats Ramdas's broken arm with earth packs and is best man at Polak's wedding.
updates.kasturba: Comes to South Africa with the children and lives with English friends as family.
updates.ramdas: Breaks his arm on the voyage at eight; his father heals it with earth poultices.
updates.polak: Lives with Gandhi; on his advice marries without waiting for money.
updates.mrspolak: Comes from England to marry Polak in a simple ceremony and joins Gandhi's household.
updates.west: Returns from Lincolnshire married, with his mother-in-law too.
updates.mrswest: Arrives at Phoenix from Leicester, beautiful 'in purity of heart'.
updates.phoenix: Becomes a little village of half a dozen families.
updates.naturecure: Earth poultices heal Ramdas's arm. Gandhi later admits these experiments carry real risks.
updates.racism: The registrar of European marriages balks at an Indian best man.

chapters.situation: Kasturbai and the children have joined Gandhi in Johannesburg, where the Polaks live with them.
chapters.summary: Guided by Ruskin, Gandhi simplifies the household. They bake unleavened bread and grind wheat on a hand-mill that he, Polak, the children and the women turn together. The family cleans its own toilet, the children nurse the sick, and the boys walk five miles a day with their father as their schooling. Gandhi admits they missed out on literary education, a grievance Harilal has aired publicly. He argues with Polak, insisting on speaking only Gujarati to his children.

updates.gandhi: Runs a simple household of hand-ground flour and self-cleaned toilets. Educates his sons on walks and insists on Gujarati.
updates.harilal: Stays behind in India and is the only son not raised in Johannesburg. Has voiced his distress over his lack of education 'privately before me and publicly in the press'.
updates.manilal: Grinds flour, cleans and nurses at home, and walks with his father to the office.
updates.ramdas: Raised in the Johannesburg household of manual labour.
updates.devdas: Raised in the Johannesburg household of manual labour.
updates.polak: Argues hard that the children should learn English, and fails to convince Gandhi.
updates.education: Gandhi admits he sacrificed his sons' literary training to service. Mother-tongue education is a point of principle.
updates.simplicity: A £7 hand-mill and baking at home.
updates.sanitation: The children clean the closet themselves and have no aversion to scavenger's work.

chapters.situation: Gandhi thought he had settled in Johannesburg with his family, when news comes of a Zulu 'rebellion' in Natal.
chapters.summary: Out of loyalty to the Empire, Gandhi offers an Indian ambulance corps. He breaks up the Johannesburg home and sends Kasturbai to Phoenix. Appointed Sergeant Major of a corps of 24, mostly ex-indentured South Indians, he finds no real rebellion: a chief opposed a new tax and a sergeant was speared. The corps nurses Zulus, flogged prisoners and 'friendlies' shot by mistake, whose wounds white nurses had refused to dress, despite abuse from white soldiers. Officers who had opposed him in 1896 thank him.

updates.gandhi: Serves six weeks as Sergeant Major of an Indian ambulance corps, nursing wounded Zulus. Marches up to 40 miles a day.
updates.kasturba: Moves to Phoenix with full consent as Gandhi breaks up the Johannesburg household.
updates.polak: Moves to a smaller house in Johannesburg and keeps some of Gandhi's belongings.
updates.booth: Gandhi's year at Booth's hospital lets him dispense medicine for white soldiers.
updates.zulu: Not a rebellion but a protest against a new tax. The corps nurses flogged suspects and mistakenly shot 'friendlies'.
updates.loyalty: Loyalty still drives Gandhi to serve, though his heart is with the Zulus.
updates.nursing: Gandhi's corps dresses the Zulus' festering wounds when white nurses will not.
updates.racism: White soldiers abuse the Zulus and try to stop the Indians nursing them.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is serving with his ambulance corps in the Zulu campaign, which he sees as a manhunt.
chapters.summary: Marching through the solitude of Zululand, Gandhi decides that serving humanity is impossible alongside family pleasures and raising children. After his discharge and the Governor's thanks, he discusses the vow with Chhaganlal, Maganlal, West and others at Phoenix. In mid-1906 he takes the vow of brahmacharya for life. He stops sharing a bed with his wife, and finds that mastering his thoughts remains hard.

updates.gandhi: Takes a lifelong vow of brahmacharya in mid-1906, aged 36, and stops sharing a bed with Kasturba.
updates.kasturba: Gandhi stops sleeping beside her after the vow.
updates.chhaganlal: Accepts the idea of brahmacharya; some at Phoenix take the vow.
updates.west: Discusses the vow; some at Phoenix succeed in keeping it.
updates.zulu: Gandhi calls it 'no war but a manhunt', with rifles going off every morning in innocent hamlets.
updates.brahmacharya: The lifelong vow is sealed in mid-1906. It begins with the body but must extend to thought.
updates.vows: 'Man is man because he is capable of… self-restraint.'

chapters.situation: Gandhi has just taken the brahmacharya vow, and events in Johannesburg are about to test it.
chapters.summary: Gandhi sees his whole life, culminating in the vow, as secret preparation for satyagraha. The movement began under the English name 'passive resistance', but Europeans took that as a weapon of the weak that could turn hateful or violent. He offers a prize in Indian Opinion for a new name. Maganlal suggests 'Sadagraha' (firmness in truth), which Gandhi changes to 'satyagraha'. He refers readers to his 'Satyagraha in South Africa' for the full history.

updates.gandhi: Satyagraha is born. Gandhi will tell its full story in 'Satyagraha in South Africa' and here gives only personal episodes.
updates.indianopinion: Runs the competition that names the movement.
updates.satyagraha: Born in 1906 in Johannesburg. Called 'passive resistance' at first, which Gandhi rejected as a 'weapon of the weak'. Renamed from Maganlal's 'Sadagraha'.

chapters.situation: Satyagraha has begun, and Gandhi wants to keep his brahmacharya vow in thought as well as deed.
chapters.summary: Diet experiments now have a religious motive. Gandhi tries fruit diets and fasts on Ekadashi and holy days. He finds fruit can indulge the palate as much as grain, and that fasting can sharpen the appetite and become 'a weapon of indulgence'. His constant companion in these experiments is Hermann Kallenbach. Gandhi later sees it was wrong for them to dwell on the pleasure of food, since one should eat only to keep the body going.

updates.gandhi: Fasts and lives on fruit to master his palate, and realizes the craving for taste follows him from food to food.
updates.kallenbach: Gandhi's constant companion in fasting and diet experiments; Gandhi lives with him at the height of the struggle.
updates.diet: The motive is now religious. Fasting can be a 'weapon of indulgence' as much as of restraint.
updates.brahmacharya: 'Passion in man is generally coexistent with a hankering after the pleasures of the palate.'
updates.satyagraha: Gandhi refines his diet to prepare for the struggle.

chapters.situation: Satyagraha is underway or about to begin. Kasturbai is gravely ill with frequent haemorrhages.
chapters.summary: Kasturbai undergoes surgery in Durban without chloroform. When she grows weaker, the doctor secretly gives her beef tea, then demands freedom to continue. Gandhi says she must decide. Too weak to sit up, she answers that she would rather die in his arms than pollute her body. Gandhi carries her through drizzling rain by rickshaw, train and hammock to Phoenix, where she slowly recovers under hydropathy. When a Swami argues from Manu that meat is permitted, Kasturbai ends the discussion herself.

updates.gandhi: Takes Kasturba from the doctor's care to Phoenix rather than allow beef tea, and carries her in his arms onto the train.
updates.kasturba: Survives an operation without anaesthetic. Refuses beef tea at death's door and comforts her husband on the risky journey. Silences a Swami's arguments: 'my mind is made up.'
updates.durbandoctor: Secretly gives Kasturbai beef tea and refuses to treat her unless free to prescribe meat.
updates.manilal: Present when the Swami argues for meat; makes light of it.
updates.ramdas: Present when the Swami argues for meat; makes light of it.
updates.west: Meets the party at Phoenix station with a hammock and six bearers.
updates.phoenix: Kasturbai recovers here under hydropathic treatment.
updates.diet: Kasturbai's faith in vegetarianism is 'unshakable' and rests on tradition, not texts.
updates.naturecure: Hydropathy at Phoenix brings Kasturbai back to health.
